
### Function headers

{{< include /chapters/coding-practices/function-documentation.qmd >}}

### Script headers

Every file in a project that doesn't have roxygen function documentation
should at least have a header that allows it to be interpreted on its own.
It should include the name of the project and a short description for what this file (among the many in your project) does specifically. 
You may optionally wish to include the inputs and outputs of the script as well, though the next section makes this significantly less necessary.

```
################################################################################
# @Organization - Example Organization
# @Project - Example Project
# @Description - This file is responsible for [...]
################################################################################

```
  
### Sections and subsections
RStudio ([v1.4 or more recent](https://blog.rstudio.com/2020/12/02/rstudio-v1-4-preview-little-things/)) supports the use of sections and subsections.
You can easily navigate through longer scripts using the navigation pane in RStudio.
Create sections and subsections with comment lines like these:

```
# Section -------

## Subsection -------

### Sub-subsection -------
```

### Code folding

Consider using RStudio's [code folding](https://support.posit.co/hc/en-us/articles/200484568-Code-Folding-and-Sections) feature to collapse and expand different sections of your code.
Any comment line with at least four trailing dashes (-), equal signs (=), or pound signs (#) automatically creates a code section.
The section headers shown above are examples.


### Comments in the body of your code

Commenting your code is an important part of reproducibility and helps document your code for the future. When things change or break, you'll be thankful for comments. There's no need to comment excessively or unnecessarily, but a comment describing what a large or complex chunk of code does is always helpful. See [this file](https://github.com/kmishra9/Flu-Absenteeism/blob/master/Master's%20Thesis%20-%20Spatial%20Epidemiology%20of%20Influenza/1b%20-%20Map-Management.R) for an example of how to comment your code and notice that comments are always in the form of:

```
# This is a comment -- first letter is capitalized and spaced away from the pound sign
```

### Variable labels {#sec-variable-labels}

Add a descriptive label as soon as you create each key variable
(any variable that might end up in a figure, table, or output model).
The label should explicitly include measurement units where applicable.

In R, prefer the [`{labelled}`](https://larmarange.github.io/labelled/) package
over raw base R attributes.
`{labelled}` integrates seamlessly with tidyverse pipelines:

```r
library(labelled)

# Set variable labels directly in a pipeline
data <- data |>
  set_variable_labels(
    blood_lead_level = "Blood lead concentration (ug/dL)",
    pm25_exposure = "Annual average PM2.5 exposure (ug/m^3)"
  )

# Set a single variable label using var_label()
var_label(data$blood_lead_level) <- "Blood lead concentration (ug/dL)"
```

Labeling key variables at the point of creation ensures that
downstream table generators
(such as [`{gtsummary}`](https://www.danieldsjoberg.com/gtsummary/))
can automatically display human-readable descriptions and correct units
without error-prone manual relabeling.

#### Read labels from the data in plots and tables {#sec-labels-from-data}

Set each label once, on the data, in preprocessing,
and let every plot and table read it from there.
Don't type a variable's label again while building a plot or table:
a second copy can drift from the first,
and the next plot of the same variable needs a third.

ggplot2 (version 4.0.0 and later) titles each axis and legend
with the label of the variable mapped to it,
so a plot of labeled data needs no `labs()` call:

```r
# Preprocessing
wages <- wages |>
  labelled::set_variable_labels(
    age = "Age (years)",
    wage = "Wage (thousands of dollars)"
  )

# Plotting: the axis titles come from the labels
wages |>
  ggplot2::ggplot() +
  ggplot2::aes(x = age, y = wage) +
  ggplot2::geom_point()
```

Not:

```r
wages |>
  ggplot2::ggplot() +
  ggplot2::aes(x = age, y = wage) +
  ggplot2::geom_point() +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Wage (thousands of dollars)")
```

A variable that a layer computes, such as the `count` of a histogram,
is not a column of the data, so it has no label attribute.
Name its label in a vector made in preprocessing,
and pass that vector as the plot's `dictionary`:

```r
wage_labels <- c(count = "Number of workers")

wages |>
  ggplot2::ggplot() +
  ggplot2::aes(x = wage) +
  ggplot2::geom_histogram() +
  ggplot2::labs(dictionary = wage_labels)
```

A table function that does not read the label attribute
takes the labels from the data:

```r
wage_names <- labelled::var_label(
  wages,
  unlist = TRUE,
  null_action = "fill"
)
knitr::kable(wages, col.names = wage_names)
```

A plot's `title`, `subtitle`, `caption`, and `alt` text describe the plot, not a variable,
so they stay in the plotting code.

`lms::hardcoded_label_linter()` flags a string literal given as a variable's label
in `labs()`, `xlab()`, `ylab()`, a scale's `name`, a guide's `title`,
`knitr::kable(col.names = )`, `DT::datatable(colnames = )`,
`gt::cols_label()`, or `flextable::set_header_labels()`
(see [`lms`](https://github.com/Morrison-Lab/psc/tree/main/lms)).

*See also [Function Structure and Documentation](coding-style.qmd#sec-function-docs) for function documentation style guidelines.*
